# Acquisition, tracking and signal retention {#sec-tracking-retention}

An estimate from a finite burst can initialize a receiver, but it cannot keep a
local reference aligned indefinitely. Feedback can follow changing phase. It can
also remove the physical phase variation we meant to measure. The engineering
question is therefore not simply how to minimize a detector error: it is how to
retain the wanted signal while controlling nuisance phase and avoiding unsupported
claims about acquisition and recovery.

We use the observation and phase conventions developed in
[Chapters 1–3](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd), and the local/global inference
distinction in [Chapter 5](phase-delay-inference.qmd). No specialist control theory
is presumed. This is a scalar continuous-time teaching model of a phase tracker,
not a complete receiver or a digital synchronization design. Inputs and targets
are illustrative. The mathematical model and local conventions do not establish
hardware performance or book-wide convention authority.

## Build the loop from its physical actions

Let theta(t) be incoming phase relative to a declared ideal carrier at a receiver
comparison plane, and let theta_hat(t) be the local oscillator's correction phase
referred to the same orientation and epoch. Its instantaneous frequency correction
is dot(theta_hat)/(2 pi) in Hz. A phase detector sees their difference plus a
small equivalent input phase error n(t). In a locked, amplitude-valid interval,
normalize the detector's slope to unity and model the correction law as

$$
 \dot{\widehat\theta}=k(\theta+n-\widehat\theta),\qquad k>0.
$$

The gain k has units s^-1: oscillator integration converts a frequency command
to phase. This is proportional feedback through an ideal oscillator. Actual detector
and actuator gains must multiply to this k after unit conversion. Saturation,
processing delay, oscillator tuning limits, fades and wrapped detector behavior
are omitted for this locked-state model. Define true residual e=theta-theta_hat;
the measured detector quantity is e+n, which has different noise statistics.

With zero initial conditions, replacing differentiation by the Laplace variable s
turns the differential equation into an algebraic equation. Solving gives

$$
 T(s)={k\over s+k},\qquad E(s)=1-T(s)={s\over s+k},
 \quad \widehat\Theta=T(\Theta+N),\qquad e=E\theta-Tn.
$$

Capital symbols denote transforms; the final relation also denotes the corresponding
linear filtering. A perturbation decays as exp(-kt), so this ideal closed loop is
stable. It has one pole at -k and time constant 1/k. A phase step Delta gives
residual Delta exp(-kt); a constant phase rate Omega gives steady residual Omega/k.
These results follow by solving dot(e)+ke=dot(theta) with n=0. They describe
linear tracking after initialization, not general capture of an unknown carrier.
The small-error replacement of a sinusoidal detector and the separation of input
phase distortion from detector noise are developed in Tausworthe's
[JPL report](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19660008034/downloads/19660008034.pdf),
Part I §§3-C and 5-A. We derive this specific normalization rather than importing
its bandwidth or power conventions.

## Trace the wanted signal before selecting bandwidth

Write theta=theta_s+theta_d, where theta_s is a wanted physical phase variation and
theta_d is nuisance reference phase. If they enter the same detector input, both
receive the same transfer. In the local oscillator phase estimate they pass through
T; in the residual they pass through E. A loop cannot infer which part is wanted
from that input alone.

For a sinusoidal phase component at offset frequency f, substitute s=j2 pi f.
Writing fc=k/(2 pi), the magnitudes are

$$
 |T|={1\over\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}},\qquad
 |E|={|f|/f_c\over\sqrt{1+(f/f_c)^2}}.
$$

Here fc is a loop corner frequency, not the RF carrier. As f tends to zero, the
estimate tracks and the residual suppresses the incoming variation. For a sensing
phase variation at 1 Hz and fc=100 Hz, residual amplitude is only 0.0099995 of
its input value. Calling that quiet residual a faithful measurement would remove
about 99 percent of the desired amplitude. The estimate output retains almost all
of it, but also retains low-frequency nuisance phase at that input. Reconstruction
by adding the estimate and true residual is an identity; the available detector
residual includes n and must be interpreted accordingly.

This is an interface decision. A communications receiver may use tracked carrier
phase to derotate a known pilot while retaining information through a separate
modulation-aware path. A phase sensor may need the correction command as part of
its reported observable. Simply choosing the narrowest or widest loop cannot
substitute for identifying where the wanted signal enters and is read out.

## Noise bandwidth and a worked tradeoff

Let n be a centered stationary phase error with two-sided density S0 rad²/Hz on
|f|<=B, zero outside. Assume stable amplitude, linear phase detection and that no
other loop noise is present. The true residual's detector-noise contribution is
-Tn, and its variance is

$$
 v_n=\int_{-B}^{B} S_0 {k^2\over k^2+(2\pi f)^2}\,df
 ={S_0k\over\pi}\tan^{-1}\left({2\pi B\over k}\right).
$$

The integral is evaluated by substituting u=2 pi f/k. For B much larger than fc,
v_n approaches S0 k/2. A locally defined one-sided equivalent noise bandwidth is
integral_0^infinity |T(j2 pi f)|² df=k/4; the two-sided integral is k/2. These
are explicit definitions in Hz, not a universal imported PLL bandwidth convention.
White phase noise over an infinite band is an idealized limiting model; the finite
B formulation keeps the observation bandwidth explicit.

Suppose a residual frequency offset of 0.5 Hz remains after coarse acquisition,
so Omega=pi rad/s. Let S0=1e-6 rad²/Hz and B=1000 Hz. The following long-time,
locked-state values exclude initial transients:

| Loop corner | Noise RMS | Steady phase bias | Root mean-square true residual |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 Hz | 0.00558712 rad | 0.050000 rad | 0.0503112 rad |
| 100 Hz | 0.0171530 rad | 0.005000 rad | 0.0178669 rad |

The last column is sqrt(v_n+(Omega/k)²), since centered noise adds variance to
the deterministic squared bias. An illustrative 0.02 rad total-RMS target rejects
the narrower loop and admits the wider one under this model. However, the wider
loop strongly suppresses a 1 Hz wanted variation at the residual output. The
receiver decision must consider both error and wanted transfer. Hardware delay,
oscillator noise and saturation could change the feasible choice; none is
validated by this calculation.

## Acquisition and nonlinear failure are separate calculations

A useful nonlinear noiseless contrast keeps the sinusoidal detector rather than
replacing it by its slope. For a constant residual frequency Omega,

$$
 \dot e=\Omega-k\sin e.
$$

A stable equilibrium in the principal interval exists for |Omega|<k at
asin(Omega/k). Its local slope is -k cos(e_eq)<0; a companion equilibrium is
unstable. At |Omega|>k no equilibrium exists and unwrapped error keeps moving,
producing slips. At equality the equilibrium attracts only from one side and gives no robust
operating margin: for Omega=k and e=pi/2+delta, dot(delta) is approximately
k delta²/2, so positive perturbations depart rather than decay. These facts are derived from this specific ideal differential
equation; they are not general capture-range specifications for real PLLs.
Noise, additional poles, delays, limits or detector ambiguities can invalidate a
capture conclusion even when the small-error transfer looks satisfactory.

For our 100 Hz candidate, Omega/k=0.005 and asin(0.005) is close to 0.005 rad.
That consistency supports the small-error approximation for the declared steady
input. It says nothing about starting with an unknown branch or near a fade.
A finite-burst phase/frequency estimate may initialize the oscillator feedforward;
feedback then follows subsequent drift. Feedforward needs its own ambiguity and
staleness assessment, while feedback needs a justified detector domain. Neither
method universally dominates.

A bounded recovery procedure must expose what is known. For this teaching case,
require an amplitude-valid record, an externally resolved phase branch, and a
coarse frequency estimate before enabling linear tracking. Choose illustrative
initial residual |e0|<=0.1 rad and |Omega|/k<=0.1. In the noiseless linear model

$$
 e(t)=e_0 e^{-kt}+{\Omega\over k}(1-e^{-kt}).
$$

Waiting 5/k reduces the initial-condition contribution to at most 0.000674 rad;
the dynamic bias remains and stochastic excursions are not bounded by that time.
Do not infer a false-lock probability or data-valid flag from this settling
calculation alone. Real validity evidence must include amplitude, innovation,
phase continuity, actuator headroom and an independent ambiguity check appropriate
to the application.

If the reference fades, freeze the last valid frequency command rather than
integrating an invalid detector output. In an illustrative holdover model with
initial phase-error bound e_max and frequency-error bound Delta_f_max, the
unwrapped phase-error bound grows as e_max+2 pi Delta_f_max t. For e_max=0.02 rad,
Delta_f_max=0.1 Hz and a 0.1 rad phase limit, holdover is at most 0.127324 s under
constant bounded frequency error. Frequency drift requires another term; unknown
restart phase defeats this continuity argument. After validity returns, repeat
coarse acquisition and ambiguity checks before reenabling the tracker. This is a
bounded interface procedure, not a tested operational acquisition policy.

As a transfer check, place latency L>0 in the entire detector-to-oscillator
feedback path. For a perturbation x about a constant-phase equilibrium, the
homogeneous equation is dot(x(t))=-k x(t-L). Trying an exponential mode
x(t)=exp(st) gives s+k exp(-sL)=0. For an oscillatory mode s=j omega, real and
imaginary parts require k cos(omega L)=0 and omega-k sin(omega L)=0. The first
positive-frequency crossing is omega=k and kL=pi/2. This is a marginal boundary Lcrit=1/(4fc): 25 ms for 10 Hz and 2.5 ms for
100 Hz. Practical margin needs further analysis. The no-delay pole at -k therefore supplies no stability
guarantee for arbitrary latency. Sampled realization, higher-order tracking,
noise-driven slip probabilities and complete system recovery sequences remain
later developments. Preserve the distinction between a locally quiet detector,
a retained physical signal and demonstrated acquisition reliability.


For a reader transfer assessment, replace the constant input phase rate with
Omega(t)=Omega0+alpha t, where alpha has units rad/s². Retain the same linear
tracker and derive its residual rather than substituting the instantaneous rate
into the constant-offset result. A particular solution is

$$
 e_p(t)={\Omega_0+\alpha t\over k}-{\alpha\over k^2};
 \qquad e(t)=e_p(t)+[e_0-e_p(0)]e^{-kt}.
$$

Substitution into dot(e)+ke=Omega0+alpha t verifies both terms. After the transient,
nonzero alpha makes error grow without bound in the linear model: eventually it
leaves the detector's small-error domain. Waiting longer does not repair dynamic
stress. Identify when a declared small-error limit would be crossed, then revise
the acquisition or tracking model before promising continued lock. During holdover,
a nonnegative bound dot_f_max on the magnitude of the relative frequency-error
derivative, in Hz/s, adds pi dot_f_max t² to the phase-error
bound. This follows by integrating 2 pi times the bounded frequency error. A
constant-offset holdover time cannot be reused unchanged under that new model.
